newsitem.title: UK: POLL-UK rates this week - analysts' quotes in full.
newsitem.headline: POLL-UK rates this week - analysts' quotes in full.

text.p: Following are some of the comments made by analysts in the Reuters poll ahead of the monetary meeting on October 30.
PHILIP SHAW, UNION DISCOUNT

"We've had disappointing inflation numbers. RPIX has been stuck in a groove and there are fewer prospects of it falling. The economy has recovered and despite an appreciation in the currency, we're likely to see inflation rising. A monetary easing would be totally inappropriate."
ALEX GARRARD, UBS

"Eddie George will probably repeat his call for a quarter point rise at the meeting and will probably cite tighter labour market conditions and wider signs of a pickup in activity as his reasons. Of course he's privately concerned that policy will be kept too loose in the run-up to the election."

"But Clarke can cite three reasons for not raising rates. Inflationary pressures on the high street are pretty subdued and surveys are indicating a similar picture. The CBI surveys are consistent with what's going to be a less than explosive recovery in activity accompanied apparently by few obvious signs of price pressure. And thirdly and perhaps most importantly is sterling's recent appreciation, some six percent since the Bank published its last inflation report and we think that will have a marked dampening on activity and prices."

"In the May 1995 inflation report the Bank reckoned that a five percent depreciation would initially, if fully passed on through import prices, add over one percent to inflation. If you reverse that ready-reckoner and if sterling strength would be sustained, the government may even be forced to concede that there's a better-than-even chance of the government achieving its target. In doing that you remove the prima facie case for a rate rise."
CHRIS TINKER, STANDARD CHARTERED

"Clarke's got a budget in three weeks' time and I think he will want to manage the mix of fiscal and monetary policy via fiscal policy. Sterling strength is taking off some of the pressure for any movement on rates and I think he will want to see the market's reaction to his budget before deciding whether the market's view is that policy is too loose or too tight."

"He'll be looking to hold rates steady for now but we'd not completely rule out the idea of a movement on rates if underlying inflation started to accelerate and the markets perceived the budget to be overly political. I think he would be prepared to tighten rates in those circumstances but certainly he's trying his damnedest to avoid having to do so."
TOM RAYNER, SOCIETE GENERALE

"Clarke's got a couple of things to help him resist calls for a rise from the Bank of England. Sterling has strengthened so fast, retail sales weren't quite as impressive as people had hoped so I think he's got enough to resist calls for higher rates. But I think we'll run into the election with unchanged rates. It's too risky."

"But we will see an increase fairly quickly regardless of who's won because Labour will have to bite the bullet and say the Tories have mismanaged things and kept monetary policy too loose. If by some miracle the Tories managed to get back in they are going to have to address the situation they've left themselves in."
KEVIN GARDINER, MORGAN STANLEY

"We'd expect rates to be rising a bit ahead of the election because the economic argument will be so powerful and so visible that for the chancellor to overrule such technocratic advice from the Bank of England would risk a political backlash. I don't think he'd do that - he's too astute a politician to risk giving the opposition and the media such an open goal. If rates rise that far ahead of the election it's possible that one increase -- if it succeeds at keeping the pound at fairly high levels -- will then keep Eddie George reasonably happy until after the election. Clarke will recognise that he can't have it both ways.
CIARAN BARR, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL

"The chancellor will acknowledge the fact that the economy is picking up. What's really holding the chancellor back is that manufacturing is only just beginning to recover. He fancies himself as a bit of an industrialist and I think he'll need to see firm signs that manufacturing is starting to benefit from a consumer-led recovery. You've got that plus continued pressure from George pushing for higher rates -- he's already calling for rates to be six percent. It's only a matter of time before he extends that -- plus the fact that Clarke wants to be seen as not playing fast and loose with the economy.
RICHARD JEFFREY, CHARTERHOUSE TILNEY

"There's a lot of pressure on Clarke to raise rates. Inflation signals have been deteriorating and that is probably recognised in the Treasury. We've got pretty strong domestic demand and I think, if he feels that a tightening is going to be appropriate at any stage before an election, it's better to get it out of the way, before the good news of the budget as well, so it strikes me that this Wednesday would be a very sensible time to raise base rates by 25 to 50 basis points".
-- Karen Iley, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 7958
